title: Consultancy agents draft scoping and solution designs from meeting transcripts
problem: Senior consultants spend hours writing technical plans and chasing spreadsheets, with scoping documents built by hand from transcripts and requirements.
approach: Certinia's Veda agents draft solution architectures and automate transcripts, requirements, backlogs and scoping at Spaulding Ridge and Diabsolut.
Spaulding Ridge: drafting time roughly 80 hours to under 20 (vendor-published); Diabsolut: documentation time 70% cut (vendor-published).
Review steps are not described in the source; the figures cover drafting, not estimate accuracy or win rate.

title: PSA agents build engagement estimates from past engagement actuals (vendor-described)
problem: Estimates for project-based services are built from templates or gut instinct, which Certinia says misses cost and risk exposure.
approach: Certinia announced Veda agents in its Salesforce-native professional services software: one builds estimates, another tracks them with expenses and risks (launched 2026-04-15).
Estimates and pricing are grounded in the actuals of prior engagements rather than templates.
Vendor headline: proposal or SOW creation from 8 hours to 1 hour (vendor-published); not specific to the estimating agents.
Human checkpoints are not described on the vendor page.

title: Fee proposals priced from the firm's own comparable past matters
problem: Fee proposals are priced by habit: in BigHand's survey, 35% say lawyers default to standard hourly rates and 28% copy a past matter's price.
approach: Ayora (now part of BigHand) and Narrative find comparable past matters, adjust for staffing and scope, and let pricing teams test scenarios.
August's demo calculates flat fees from uploaded invoices and prior bills; a lawyer drafts the client email.
Vendor claim for firms using its product: realisation up 2-4%; about 10% more new work won (vendor-published).

title: Fixed-fee quotes checked against anonymised market ranges before pricing a matter
problem: Goodwin's clients push for efficiency and predictability, and the firm wants to answer pricing and budgeting requests faster.
approach: Goodwin announced a global rollout of PERSUIT's Fixed-Fee Price Benchmarking, returning a range of typical fees from anonymised historical proposals and matters.
The vendor says it does not set or recommend prices; lawyers and pricing staff choose the price and the client negotiates independently.
Goodwin says it can respond to pricing requests more quickly; no measurement published (self-reported).

title: Agent drafts the statement of work from sales context
problem: Sales and delivery teams re-key deal context into statements of work (the document fixing scope, deliverables and fees) by hand, which slows proposals and weakens the handoff.
approach: Certinia's SOW Drafter Agent generates a statement of work from sales context so delivery starts aligned.
Neocol brought its entire sales team live on the workflow within nine days of launch (vendor-published); no drafting-time measurement published.
Review steps are not described; Certinia calls the outputs polished drafts.

title: Hourly matters: budget and bill the time AI-assisted work actually takes
problem: Hourly budgets built on pre-AI task times are a compliance risk, because several bar opinions say an hourly fee must reflect time actually spent.
approach: Norton Rose Fulbright says it bills hours actually worked, not what work might have taken without AI, and expects recovered time redirected.
Bar guidance says to budget from the effort of AI-assisted work and state in fee agreements how AI affects rates.
Billing partner reviews the pre-bill against time worked; lawyers verify AI outputs. No savings figure published (self-reported).

title: Fee agreements that state AI use, client approval and AI cost treatment
problem: Fee agreements are often silent on whether AI is used and how its cost is treated, while regulators separate overhead from matter-specific costs.
approach: Engagement letters say whether AI is used, whether client approval is needed, and which AI costs are overhead or billed at cost.
Idea: a possible shift to consumption-based AI pricing, discussed at ILTACON 2026, would force choices on which costs sit in fees.
Firms requiring client approval before using generative AI: 8% (under 50 lawyers) to 38% (350-699 lawyers) (independent).
Billing partner confirms disclosure and client consent before AI costs are charged.
who: Bar opinions and surveys; no named firm

title: Predictive alerts on matters heading over budget, tracking work in progress
problem: Budgets are set but few firms manage them actively, so overruns become write-offs; in BigHand's survey only 23% actively monitor budgets throughout a matter.
approach: Ayora tracks budgets, work in progress, billing and collections against benchmarks from past matters and issues predictive alerts on matters at risk.
Narrative describes live work in progress against budget and catching overruns before write-off (vendor descriptions).
Survey baseline: 23% actively monitor and update budgets throughout (vendor-published); the matter team acts on alerts and agrees re-scoping with the client.

title: Matter-level evidence of AI use and savings to answer client pricing questions
problem: Clients ask how AI saves them money, but firms are still gathering data, call return measurement anecdotal, and struggle to capture AI work in time records.
approach: Laurel and Legora announced on 2026-10-13 that each task completed in Legora becomes a draft time entry for the lawyer to review.
A second phase will develop, with customers, measures of how Legora is used and the value of AI-powered work.
Nearly 60% of in-house counsel see no savings yet from outside counsel's generative AI use (vendor-published).

title: Partners lead the AI-value conversation with clients before conceding on fees
problem: Few partners discuss AI with clients: over one-third of stand-out lawyers in Thomson Reuters Institute's survey talked about it with under 20% of their clients.
approach: Thomson Reuters Institute recommends partners lead with what changed for the client, agree how AI is used, then discuss pricing.
DLA Piper's AI innovation head advised firms to lead the conversation before the client sets the terms.
The partner owns the client conversation; client general counsel and firm leadership agree any pilot terms.
About one-third of embedded AI partners have discussed AI with at least 60% of their clients (vendor-published).

title: Clients write AI-savings terms into outside-counsel guidelines and press suppliers on fees
problem: In-house teams cannot see what AI savings they get, with nearly 60% of surveyed in-house counsel seeing no noticeable savings yet.
approach: In-house teams ask how AI saves money, request AI invoice line items, and add guideline terms reflecting time saved in billed hours.
In one reported case KPMG pressed its auditor Grant Thornton to cut its fee, arguing AI should make the audit more efficient.
Reported fee reduction: 14% (about $416,000 in 2024 to about $357,000 in 2025) (independent).
Client counsel agree the guideline provisions; fees are negotiated between buyer and supplier.
who: KPMG, Grant Thornton, in-house legal teams

title: Public-sector buyers recover consulting fees after AI errors and require AI-use declarations
problem: A government-commissioned consulting report contained apparent AI-generated errors, including a fabricated court quotation, so government buyers cannot tell whether fees reflect AI use.
approach: Deloitte reviewed the 237-page report and confirmed some footnotes and references were incorrect; a revised version discloses generative AI use.
The Australian department said Deloitte agreed to repay the final instalment of an AUD 440,000 contract; amount to be made public (independent).
Australia's Public Service AI plan (12 Nov 2025) says advisory-panel suppliers will have to advise planned AI use in quote responses.

title: Performance metrics moved off billed hours so non-hourly pricing can work
problem: When staff are paid and promoted on billed hours, AI efficiency is not rewarded and value pricing meets internal resistance.
approach: Wipfli is introducing non-traditional metrics such as client satisfaction and cycle time as pricing and technology change.
Resultsense reports PwC senior-staff bonuses will track revenue and margin per professional rather than hours billed (secondary report).
A GGI commentary says compensation, origination credit and write-off policy must change if non-hourly pricing is to work.

title: Idea: choose the fee structure by how observable outcomes and costs are
problem: Idea, not a deployment: pricing models are chosen by convention, and only 7.3% of resource-management respondents say outcome data is easily accessible and routinely used in staffing.
approach: Brynjolfsson and Petropoulos propose asking per engagement whether the client can verify and attribute results, and see the firm's true delivery cost.
The answers map onto time-based, project, subscription, outcome or hybrid pricing, with hybrid treated as the equilibrium.
At scoping, agree metrics, baselines and where possible controlled rollouts before tying any fee to outcomes; an executive approves the structure.

title: Flat or alternative fees for repeatable legal work, pricing in AI savings
problem: Under hourly billing AI efficiency cuts a firm's own revenue; one author's arithmetic has a task falling from 1 hour to 0.2 hours removing 80% of that revenue.
approach: Firms move repeatable matters to flat or alternative fees and build expected AI time savings into the price, with phase-based scoping.
Partner and pricing team set scope, fee and re-scoping triggers; the client agrees success measures before the engagement.
Survey: 30% keep existing pricing and take the profit; 25% offer discounts when clients permit AI use (vendor-published).
54% of UK firms expect more fixed-fee billing (vendor-published).

title: Accounting firms pilot value-based and subscription pricing as AI shortens work
problem: AI can halve the time to produce a client report, forcing a choice between keeping the saving as margin or passing it on as a lower price.
approach: Per Bloomberg Tax, leaders at KPMG, PwC and RSM are brainstorming charging on value and outcomes; RSM uses several pricing models.
RKL is piloting a value-based model created by consultancy Fore LLC and has onboarded several dozen new clients (self-reported).
RSM's example: certain tax advisory reports fall from 20 hours to 10 with generative AI and checking (self-reported).
The partner prices on the value the client attaches to the work.
who: RSM, RKL, PwC, KPMG, Fore LLC

title: Deciding where the AI time dividend goes: price, margin, advisory or quality
problem: AI saves delivery time, but if price stays tied to hours the saving is lost or handed to the client.
approach: Thomson Reuters Institute describes three paths for tax firms: redeploy people to advisory, serve more clients, or rebuild around continuous insight.
Thomson Reuters' 2026 survey describes an Elevate path, preferred by 52% of professionals surveyed: AI raises quality, fees held or raised.
Firms saying AI saves them time: 84.8% (independent).
Partners and pricing leads decide whether savings become margin, price reduction or new services.

title: KPI-based monthly retainer billing replaces hourly billing for insurance-defence work
problem: Under hourly billing, faster work cuts the firm's revenue, while insurer clients audit and cut bills line by line, costing both sides administrative effort.
approach: Kopka Law moves defence-litigation clients to monthly retainer or portfolio billing judged on KPIs such as cycle time and indemnity outcome.
It uses the insurer's claim frequency and severity data and its own litigation-category data to set the arrangement.
Firm reports freed capital and administrative resources; no figures published (self-reported). How KPIs are set and reviewed is not described.

title: Management consultancy ties a share of fees to client outcomes
problem: Clients arrive with a result they want rather than a defined scope, and AI-compressed analytical work makes hours harder to defend.
approach: McKinsey says clients bring a target outcome and the fee is mostly contingent on performance against a scorecard, with some fixed components.
Its UK managing partner said in November 2025 that about a quarter of global fees come from outcome-based pricing (self-reported).
The scorecard is agreed with the client before work starts, and the client signs off results.

title: IT services firms shift contracts from hours to outcomes, sharing AI savings
problem: Clients demand price cuts as AI lifts delivery efficiency, and billing large offshore workforces by the hour loses its logic.
approach: Reuters reports TCS, Infosys, Wipro, HCLTech and Cognizant increasingly tie fees to performance outcomes instead of hours worked.
TCS's CEO said about 80% of contracts in one segment use outcome performance measures (self-reported).
Persistent's CEO said clients were demanding the same work for 25% to 30% less (self-reported).
Reuters, citing people familiar, says a Cognizant-Daimler Truck deal splits AI-related cost savings between vendor and client.

title: AI-native law firms sell fixed-price bundles or per-document rates instead of hours
problem: Routine commercial contract work is priced by the hour at traditional firms; Falcon's founders say straightforward work can cost small and medium businesses EUR 3,000 to 4,000 a piece.
approach: Falcon (Belgium) offers six contract reviews a month for a flat EUR 1,000, each signed off by a qualified lawyer, same day.
Crosby advertises fixed rates by the document, with human attorneys reviewing all work.
Falcon's founders estimate EUR 3,000-4,000 per straightforward piece of work at a traditional firm (self-reported).

title: PwC One packages expertise into AI-delivered services, possibly priced by subscription
problem: Hours-based billing built on large junior teams doing routine tasks is threatened when AI can do much of that work.
approach: PwC introduced PwC One on 2026-03-19: clients describe a problem, agents do the work, PwC professionals review outputs; beta in March 2026.
Press coverage says some services may become tools clients access directly, potentially by annual subscription; PwC's release gives no pricing.
Six automated services at launch, with more promised; no price, uptake or quality figure published (self-reported).

title: Law firms license firm-built AI tools to clients and peers
problem: Clients want AI-enabled service but see little of what firms do, and hours are no way to charge for a tool.
approach: Debevoise's STAAR gives clients the firm's AI-risk guidance; ABA Journal reports STAAR 2.0 as a subscription platform built with Legora.
A&O Shearman has a revenue-sharing arrangement with Harvey to license its tools to clients and other firms.
Cooley made Cooley GO Lab, a Legora-built workspace, free to a summer Y Combinator cohort.
Debevoise says the tools complement its lawyers' advice. No figures published (self-reported).
who: Debevoise, A&O Shearman, Cooley, Legora, Harvey
